title: Parent education, attachment and safe sleep
blurb: Prepare parents for birth and parenthood, promote attachment, advise on going-to-sleep position in pregnancy and give safe infant sleep advice, including bed-sharing.
question: Danielle is breastfeeding her 5-day-old son. At a home visit she says she had two glasses of wine at a family party this evening and plans to bring the baby into bed with her tonight. What should the midwife advise?

teach.h: Getting ready to be a parent
teach.body: Preparing for parenthood is more than a birth plan. NICE asks midwives to talk through the physical and emotional changes of pregnancy, changes in relationships, how partners can support each other, and how parents can bond with their baby. Attachment is the emotional tie between a baby and the people who care for it; it grows when parents notice and respond to the baby's cues. SPM 3.9 asks midwives to promote parent and newborn mental health, positive attachment and the transition to parenthood.

items.label: Care plan, diet, smoking, alcohol, activity
Sleep on side; labour, newborn care, feeding, mood

teach.caption: NG194 1.3.17: face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding to the baby's cues.

teach.h: Bonding: what helps and what gets in the way
teach.caption: Extra support may be needed by parents who were in care, had adverse childhood experiences, a traumatic birth or complex psychosocial needs (NG194 1.3.19).

teach.h: Going to sleep on her side after 28 weeks
teach.body: NICE NG201 advises women to avoid going to sleep on their back after 28 weeks and to consider pillows to stay on their side, explaining there may be a link between going to sleep on the back and stillbirth in late pregnancy. The advice is about the position she falls asleep in. The baby, by contrast, is always put down on its back.

children.label: Strongly advise against
children.sub: Low birth weight; parent had 2+ units, smokes, drowsy medicine or drugs

children.label: Safer bed-sharing
children.sub: Firm flat mattress, face up, no pillows or duvet near baby, no pets or other children

teach.body: Danielle has had 2 or more units of alcohol, so NICE NG194 says to strongly advise her not to share a bed with her baby tonight. The midwife says this kindly and practically: put him on his back in his own clear cot in her room, and do not fall asleep with him on the sofa. On other nights, with no risk factors, she explains the safer bed-sharing steps. The advice is recorded.

teach.text: Woman on her SIDE to sleep in late pregnancy; baby on its BACK for every sleep. And the most dangerous place to fall asleep with a baby is a sofa or armchair, which is far riskier than a planned, safer bed-share.

items: Discuss changes, relationships and bonding throughout pregnancy; offer classes to nulliparous women and partners.
Attachment grows from skin-to-skin, face-to-face time and responding to cues; some parents need extra support.
After 28 weeks, advise going to sleep on her side (possible link between back sleeping and stillbirth).
Babies sleep on their back in a clear, flat cot in the parents' room for at least 6 months, room 16–20 °C.
Strongly advise against bed-sharing if the baby was low birth weight or a parent has had 2+ units, smokes, or took sedating medicine or drugs.

summary: You can now plan parent education across pregnancy, promote attachment and spot families who need extra support, and give clear advice on going-to-sleep position after 28 weeks. You can also give safe infant sleep advice and know when to strongly advise against bed-sharing.

A.q: After 28 weeks of pregnancy, how does NICE NG201 advise a woman to go to sleep?
options: On her back, raised on pillows
On her front, with a pillow
A.why: NG201 1.3.25–1.3.26: avoid going to sleep on the back after 28 weeks (possible link with stillbirth); pillows can help maintain the side position.

whyNot.0: Going to sleep on her back is what NICE advises against.
whyNot.1: Front sleeping is not the advised position in late pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Semi-reclined on her back is still back sleeping; NICE advises going to sleep on her side.

A.q: Parents ask how to put their newborn down to sleep. What is the correct advice?
options: On the side, propped with a towel
On the back, in a clear flat cot
On the front, to reduce reflux
On the back, with a small pillow
A.why: Lullaby Trust and NG194: babies sleep on their back for every sleep, on a firm flat surface with no pillows, duvets or bumpers.

whyNot.0: Side sleeping is less safe than back sleeping, and towels add risk.
whyNot.3: Pillows should not be in a baby's sleep space.

A.q: Which factor means parents should be strongly advised not to share a bed with their baby?
options: The baby is over three months old
A.why: NICE NG194 1.3.15: strongly advise against bed-sharing if the baby was low birth weight or either parent has had 2+ units of alcohol, smokes, has taken sedating medicine or used recreational drugs.

whyNot.0: Breastfeeding is protective, not a reason to avoid bed-sharing.
whyNot.1: Age over three months is not one of the NG194 risk factors.

B.q: To whom does NICE NG201 say antenatal classes should be offered?
options: Women who request them in writing
B.why: NG201 1.3.20: offer nulliparous women (and their partners) antenatal classes; consider them for multiparous women who could benefit (1.3.21).

whyNot.1: Classes are not limited to high-risk pregnancies.
whyNot.2: Young women may have tailored services, but the NG201 offer is to all nulliparous women.
whyNot.3: Classes are offered proactively, not on written request.

B.q: Which approach does NICE NG194 encourage to promote emotional attachment?
options: Strict feeding times to build routine
Letting the baby settle without comfort
B.why: NG194 1.3.17: encourage face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin contact and responding appropriately to the baby's cues.

whyNot.0: Responsive care, not strict schedules, supports attachment.
whyNot.1: Responding to cues builds a secure bond.
whyNot.3: Babies cannot be 'spoiled' by responsive handling; contact supports attachment.

B.q: Which parents does NICE NG194 identify as possibly needing extra support with bonding and attachment?
options: Parents who were in the care system
Parents who planned a home birth
B.why: NG194 1.3.19: extra support may be needed by parents who have been through the care system, had adverse childhood experiences, a traumatic birth or complex psychosocial needs.

whyNot.0: Parental age over 30 is not listed as a factor.
whyNot.2: Having a second baby is not a listed factor.
whyNot.3: Planned place of birth is not a listed factor.

C.q: Danielle is breastfeeding her 5-day-old son. She had two glasses of wine at a party this evening and plans to bring him into bed tonight. What is the best advice?
options: Bed-share with the baby face up, no pillows
Sleep with him on the sofa instead of the bed
Bed-share with him between both parents
C.why: NG194 1.3.15: a parent who has had 2 or more units of alcohol should be strongly advised not to bed-share. He should sleep on his back in his own cot in her room.

whyNot.0: Safer bed-sharing steps apply when there are no risk factors; alcohol is one.
whyNot.2: Sleeping on a sofa with a baby is more dangerous than a bed.
whyNot.3: Placing him between two adults adds risk and ignores the alcohol.

C.q: On a day-10 visit, the midwife finds a baby asleep on his back in a cot with a pillow and a thick duvet. The room is 24 °C. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Turn him onto his side to stop choking
Move the cot into a separate room
Remove the bedding and cool the room
Add a hat, as babies lose heat
C.why: Lullaby Trust: a clear, flat cot with no pillows or duvets, and a room temperature of 16–20 °C. He is already correctly on his back.

whyNot.0: Back sleeping is correct; side sleeping is less safe.
whyNot.1: Babies should sleep in the parents' room for at least the first 6 months.
whyNot.3: A hat indoors adds to overheating, which is already a concern.

C.q: Laila, 32 weeks pregnant, is anxious because she woke up on her back last night. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Set alarms to check her position overnight
Sleep propped upright in a chair
Back sleeping is safe until 36 weeks
Go to sleep on her side, using pillows
C.why: NG201 1.3.25: advise women to avoid going to sleep on their back after 28 weeks and to consider pillows to help maintain their position, so she goes to sleep on her side. The advice concerns the position she goes to sleep in.

whyNot.0: NICE advice is about the going-to-sleep position, not overnight waking.
whyNot.1: Sleeping in a chair is not advised and disturbs rest.
whyNot.2: The advice applies from 28 weeks, not 36.

reteach.title: Side for her, back for baby
reteach.question: Can you keep the two sleep positions straight, and know when a bed-share is unsafe?

blocks.body: In late pregnancy the woman goes to sleep on her side. After birth the baby sleeps on its back, in a clear flat cot in the parents' room. Bed-sharing is strongly advised against if the baby was low birth weight, or a parent has drunk 2 or more units, smokes, or has taken sedating medicine or drugs.

blocks.text: A sofa or armchair is the most dangerous place to fall asleep with a baby.

explain.body: Discuss changes, relationships and bonding throughout pregnancy. After 28 weeks cover labour, baby care, feeding, vitamin K, newborn screening and mood. Offer classes to nulliparous women and partners (NG201).

test.q: From when does NG201 suggest discussing preparation for labour, newborn care and feeding?
test.why: NG201 1.3.15: after 28 weeks, discuss preparing for labour and birth, care of the new baby, feeding and postnatal topics.

whyNot.0: Booking focuses on the plan of care and lifestyle.
whyNot.1: 16 weeks is earlier than NG201 places this discussion.
whyNot.3: From 38 weeks the focus is prolonged pregnancy.

explain.body: Face-to-face interaction, skin-to-skin and responding to cues build attachment. Recovery, fatigue, traumatic birth and feeding worries can get in the way (NG194 1.3.16–1.3.19).

test.q: Which is listed by NICE NG194 as a challenge that may affect bonding?
test.why: NG194 1.3.18: challenges include physical and emotional recovery, traumatic birth, fatigue and sleep deprivation, feeding concerns and the demands of parenthood.

whyNot.0: Breastfeeding itself is not listed as a challenge (feeding concerns are).

explain.body: After 28 weeks, advise avoiding going to sleep on the back, using pillows to stay on the side; explain the possible link with stillbirth (NG201 1.3.25–1.3.26).

test.q: From which gestation should women be advised to avoid going to sleep on their back?

whyNot.0: 20 weeks is earlier than the NICE advice.
whyNot.1: 24 weeks is earlier than the NICE advice.
whyNot.2: 36 weeks is later than the NICE advice.

explain.body: Back to sleep in a clear, flat cot, room-sharing for at least 6 months, room 16–20 °C. Strongly advise against bed-sharing with risk factors (NG194 1.3.15).

test.q: For how long should a baby sleep in the same room as the parents?
test.why: Lullaby Trust: room-share for at least the first 6 months.

whyNot.3: Two years goes well beyond the advice.
